extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners/patent attorneys preparing/responding to Office actions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. §103, including when and how to rely on prior art combinations, implicit disclosures, scientific theory, common knowledge/official notice, and legal precedent; plus indicia of obviousness (e.g., omissions, scaling, rearrangement, purification, overlapping ranges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale for combining references
rubrics_metrics.description: The strongest rationale for combining references is a recognition, expressly or impliedly in the prior art, or drawn from a convincing line of reasoning based on established scientific principles or legal precedent, that some advantage or expected beneficial result would have been produced by their combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit motivation exists when a suggestion may be gleaned from the prior art as a whole; combinations that yield a product or process that is more desirable (stronger, cheaper, cleaner, faster, lighter, smaller, more durable, or more efficient) can show motivation to combine even absent an explicit hint in the references. See In re Sernaker; Dystar Textilfarben GmbH v. C.H. Patrick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal precedent similarity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal precedent can provide the rationale supporting obviousness only if the facts in the prior legal decision are sufficiently similar to those in the application under examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must apply the law consistently and may use the court's rationale only when the factual circumstances align; if applicant demonstrates criticality of a specific limitation, it is inappropriate to rely solely on court rationale. (See In re Eli Lilly & Co.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of a rationale different from applicant's
rubrics_metrics.description: The reason or motivation to modify a reference need not match the applicant’s stated purpose; motivation may arise from addressing the general problem confronting the inventor rather than the specific problem solved by the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of ordinary skill need not see the identical problem addressed in prior art to be motivated to apply its teachings. Prior art used for different purposes can nonetheless support an obviousness rejection (e.g., In re Kahn; In re Lintner; In re Dillon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit disclosure (inferences from a reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering a reference’s disclosure, it is proper to take into account not only specific teachings but also the inferences a person skilled in the art would reasonably draw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a reference teaching a process at one temperature but recognizing higher temperatures can imply those higher temperatures (In re Preda); a generic statement like 'at least one methylene group' implies other R groups may be present (In re Lamberti).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on scientific theory
rubrics_metrics.description: An obviousness rationale may rely on logic and sound scientific principle, but when an examiner relies on a scientific theory the existence and meaning of that theory must be provided and supported by evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unsupported chemical or technical theories are inadequate to establish prima facie obviousness (see In re Grose and related cases). If relying on theory, provide evidentiary support showing the theory applies to the claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule for taking official notice / relying on common knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may take official notice of facts not in the record or rely on 'common knowledge' in making a rejection only in limited, judicious circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer citing prior art rather than taking official notice. Official notice without documentary evidence should be rare, especially when the application is under final rejection or action. See MPEP §2144.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: When official notice without documentary evidence is permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: Official notice without documentary evidence is permissible only where the facts asserted to be well-known or common knowledge are capable of instant and unquestionable demonstration as being well-known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where notice was appropriate: matters of obvious/common practice (In re Ahlert), basic facts readily verifiable or supported by references of record. In a first Office action it may be reasonable to take notice of dependent claim limitations that are old and well known expedients, provided they are of notorious character and merely 'fill in the gaps.'

rubrics_metrics.name: When it is inappropriate to take official notice
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not appropriate to take official notice of facts that are not capable of instant and unquestionable demonstration, especially technical facts in esoteric technology or specific prior art knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical assertions must be supported by citations to standard reference works or documentary evidence. Examiners should not rely solely on their own understanding or 'common sense' as principal evidence (see Zurko, In re Grose, In re Eynde, Arendi v. Apple).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to state clear technical reasoning if notice is taken
rubrics_metrics.description: If official notice is taken of a fact unsupported by documentary evidence, the technical line of reasoning underlying the decision to take such notice must be clear and unmistakable and set forth explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must provide specific factual findings based on sound technical/scientific reasoning so the applicant can adequately traverse the assertion in the next reply. Older cases accepted notice when other references supported the noticed fact or nothing in the record contradicted it (In re Soli, In re Chevenard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to support findings if applicant traverses
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant traverses a factual assertion as not properly noticed or not properly based on common knowledge, the examiner must support the finding with adequate documentary evidence in the next Office action to maintain the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must specifically point out the supposed errors; a general allegation of patentability is inadequate. If relying on personal knowledge, the examiner must provide an affidavit or declaration setting forth specific factual statements and explanations (37 CFR 1.104(d)(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finality of next Office action when relying on common knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the next Office action should be made final when common-knowledge findings are involved: if a newly added reference only supports a prior common-knowledge finding and does not introduce a new issue, the Office action may be made final; otherwise it should not be made final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no claim amendments are made, examiner must not rely on other teachings of the newly cited reference when making the action final. If the newly cited reference introduces a new ground or issues not necessitated by applicant’s amendment, the action should not be final. See MPEP §706.07(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary restriction on use of common knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Any rejection based on assertions that a fact is well-known or common knowledge in the art without documentary evidence should be judiciously applied; it is never appropriate to rely solely on common knowledge without evidentiary support as the principal evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facts so noticed should be of notorious character and serve only to fill insubstantial gaps in the evidentiary showing. See Zurko, Ahlert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic design changes (ornamentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Matters relating to ornamentation only, which have no mechanical function, cannot be relied upon to patentably distinguish the claimed invention from the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, if the shape or ornamentation results in a product distinct from the reference product (i.e., produces new/important result), it may be significant (compare In re Seid and Ex parte Hilton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of an element and its function is obvious when function not desired
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of an element and its function is obvious if the function of the element is not desired in the claimed context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include deleting components whose function is unnecessary for the claimed environment; courts have affirmed rejections where omission was an obvious expedient (Ex parte Wu; In re Larson; In re Kuhle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of an element with retention of the element's function indicates nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: If an element is omitted but its function is retained by another feature, this is an indicium of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retention of the original function despite omission can show nonobviousness (In re Edge — elimination of a transparent layer while retaining its protective function via a different structure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Automating a manual activity is generally insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadly providing an automatic or mechanical means to replace a manual activity which accomplishes the same result is not sufficient to distinguish over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replacing manual steps with timers, solenoids, or automation that achieves identical outcomes is insufficient absent new/unexpected results (In re Venner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in size/proportion or mere scaling are ordinarily obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere changes in size, proportion, or scaling up (or down) of a known process or device, if the device would perform the same, do not establish patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scaling up a process or recitation of relative dimensions without functional differences is prima facie obvious (In re Rose; In re Rinehart; Gardner v. TEC Syst., Inc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in shape are usually obvious absent persuasive evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Configuration or shape that is a matter of choice is obvious unless persuasive evidence shows the specific configuration is significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have found claimed configurations to be obvious when they are routine design choices (In re Dailey), unless the configuration imparts a functional difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in sequence of process steps are prima facie obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of any order of performing process steps is prima facie obvious in the absence of new or unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversing or altering the sequence of adding ingredients or steps is generally obvious unless it yields unexpected outcomes (Ex parte Rubin; In re Burhans; In re Gibson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Making portable/integral/separable/adjustable/continuous is normally obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Modifications such as making a device portable, integral, separable, adjustable, or continuous are ordinarily obvious unless they produce new or unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subexamples: making a device portable is not sufficient by itself (In re Lindberg); making parts integral may be mere engineering choice (In re Larson) but could be patentable if it yields insight contrary to expectations (Schenck v. Nortron); making continuous vs. batch is often obvious (In re Dilnot).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal, duplication, or rearrangement of parts is ordinarily obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal, duplication, or mere rearrangement of parts or their positions is typically an obvious modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have treated shifting positions, duplicating parts, or reversing motion as design choices lacking patentable significance absent new results (In re Gazda; In re Harza; In re Japikse; In re Kuhle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purifying an old product does not automatically render it nonobvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure forms of known products may be patentable, but mere purity by itself does not render the product nonobvious; consider whether prior art suggests the claimed form/structure or methods to obtain it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free-flowing vs. crystalline forms, purification to homogeneity, and product-by-process claims require analysis of whether prior art suggested the form or how to obtain it; purity improvements without structural or functional difference usually do not confer patentability (In re Bergstrom; In re Cofer; Purdue Pharma v. Epic Pharma). See MPEP §2113 and Ex parte Stern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness of overlapping, approaching, or similar ranges/amounts/proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed ranges 'overlap or lie inside ranges disclosed by the prior art' or are merely close to prior art ranges, a prima facie case of obviousness exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlapping ranges, or ranges close enough that one skilled in the art would expect similar properties, support prima facie obviousness (In re Wertheim; In re Woodruff; In re Geisler; Titanium Metals Corp. of America v. Banner; Warner-Jenkinson; In re Aller). See MPEP §2131.03 for related case law.
